column1: Reconstruct the Third Man argument and Aristotle's diagnosis of it.
column2:
Source: Aristotle's lost On Ideas, known through Alexander of Aphrodisias, a late paraphrase.
Premises: when many things are called "man," the Platonist posits one Form, Man itself, existing apart; the Form is itself a man (self-predication); the Form differs from the particulars (non-identity).
Conclusion: the Form and the men are again many with one name, so a further Form is needed, a "third man", without end.
Diagnosis (Met. Z.13): a universal is a "such" and not a "this", so substance is in the thing, not apart from it.
Objection: Cherniss argued Aristotle misreads Plato, and many deny Plato held self-predication in this sense; and is Aristotle's own form universal or particular?
Reply (the literature's): the real target is separation, which makes a Form another individual (Fine); the form question stays open.

column1: Reconstruct Aristotle's elenctic defence of the principle of non-contradiction (Met. Γ.3–4).
column2:
Principle: "the same attribute cannot at the same time belong and not belong to the same subject and in the same respect" (Γ.3, 1005b19–20, Ross).
Premises: not everything can be proved, on pain of regress; so ask the opponent only to say something significant; a word has one meaning, or a limited number; if "man" means two-footed animal, a man cannot also not be one.
Conclusion: whoever speaks significantly already relies on the principle, which is indemonstrable but cannot be coherently denied.
Objection: premise 4 seems to beg the question (Łukasiewicz); dialetheists such as Priest hold that some contradictions are true.
Reply (Aristotle's): in an elenctic proof the opponent supplies the assumption; the claim is only that significant speech presupposes the principle.

column1: Reconstruct the sea battle argument (De Int. 9) and Aristotle's way out.
column2:
Fatalist premises: of two contradictory statements one is true (bivalence); so one of "there will be a sea battle tomorrow" and its denial is already true; what was always true happens necessarily; then there is no need to deliberate.
But deliberation does affect the future and some things can go either way, so a premise must go.
Resolution: what is must be when it is, but not without qualification; the disjunction is necessary, neither half is.
Readings: deny bivalence for future contingents (traditional; Łukasiewicz); keep it and find a modal fallacy (Anscombe); or deny that either half is definitely true (Boethius).
Objection and reply: each reading strains the text and none is agreed; common to all, a prediction's truth does not fix the future.

column1: Reconstruct the syllogism and its reduction to the first figure (Prior Analytics I.1–7).
column2:
Definition (I.1): discourse in which, certain things being stated, something else follows of necessity.
Premises: each premise says A belongs to all, none, some or not all of B; some premises convert; the middle term stands in three figures; only first-figure syllogisms are perfect, needing nothing beyond what is stated; the others are perfected by conversion or reductio ad impossibile.
Conclusion: the whole system rests on Barbara and Celarent plus the conversion rules.
Readings: an axiomatic system (Łukasiewicz) or natural deduction (Corcoran, Smiley), now more common; Corcoran showed a formal model sound and complete.
Objection: it cannot represent relations (De Morgan's horse's head) or whole propositions, and Frege's 1879 logic replaced it.
Reply (the literature's): true, but within its fragment it is rigorous and makes logic a science.

column1: Reconstruct the argument for the four causes (Phys. II.3, II.7).
column2:
Premises: we do not think we know a thing until we grasp why it is; "why?" is answered in four ways: the material cause (the bronze of a statue), the formal cause (form or essence), the efficient cause (the sculptor or the father) and the final cause (that for the sake of which, as health is the cause of walking about); one thing has several causes; none reduces to another.
Conclusion: a full explanation gives all four. In natural things the last three often coincide, since man generates man.
Objection: Bacon and the mechanical philosophy kept only matter in motion and efficient causes; formal and final causes merely redescribe.
Reply (the literature's): these are kinds of explanation, not forces; chemistry explains by structure, and biology still asks what an organ is for.

column1: Reconstruct Aristotle's teleology against Empedocles (Phys. II.8).
column2:
Rival view: nature may work as rain falls, of necessity, and animals whose parts happened to be useful survived while the rest perished, as Empedocles says.
Premises: things happen either by chance or for an end; the parts of living things come about always or for the most part in the same way; nothing that happens by chance happens always or for the most part.
Conclusion: the parts of living things come about for an end. Support: nature works like art, nature makes mistakes, and purpose needs no deliberation, as with a doctor doctoring himself.
Objection: Darwin's natural selection explains regularity without ends.
Reply (the literature's): Empedocles' view has no inheritance or gradual accumulation; and on the Gotthelf-Cooper reading organs are still explained by what they are for.

column1: Reconstruct the definition of change as the actuality of the potential as such (Phys. III.1).
column2:
Aim: against Parmenides, show change is real and definable without contradiction.
Premises: some things are potentially what they are not yet actually; a thing can be actually one thing and potentially another; change is neither the bare potentiality nor the finished actuality, nor the actuality of the bronze as bronze.
Conclusion: "The fulfilment of what exists potentially, in so far as it exists potentially, is motion" (201a10–11, Hardie and Gaye).
Readings: entelecheia as actualization (Ross), which threatens circularity, or as actuality (Kosman): the buildable at work as buildable is the building.
Objection: Locke mocked the scholastic formula as jargon; motion is a simple, indefinable idea.
Reply (the literature's): it answers Parmenides, gives the Physics one structure for change, and grounds the unmoved mover.

column1: Reconstruct the definition of soul as first actuality (De Anima II.1).
column2:
Premises: substance is matter, form or the compound, and matter is potentiality, form actuality; living bodies are compounds; the body has life, so it is the matter and the soul the form; form is actuality; the soul is first actuality, a capacity possessed, since a sleeping animal is alive; such a body has organs.
Conclusion: the soul is "the first grade of actuality of a natural body having life potentially in it" (412a27–28, J. A. Smith), so asking whether soul and body are one is like asking about the wax and its stamped shape.
Objection (Ackrill): a living body cannot be identified without its soul, so the bronze-and-statue model fails.
Reply (partly Aristotle's, partly the literature's): seeds have life potentially; and remote matter, flesh and elements, outlasts the soul as a corpse.

column1: Reconstruct the argument for the active intellect (De Anima III.5), and why it is disputed.
column2:
Premises: every natural class has a matter-like factor and a productive cause; the soul has both; the mind of III.4, which becomes its objects, is the matter-like one; so a second mind makes all things, as light makes potential colours actual; being activity, it "is separable, impassible, unmixed" (430a17–18, J. A. Smith).
Conclusion: this mind alone is immortal and eternal, and without it nothing thinks.
Readings: Alexander made it god; Averroes one separate intellect for the species; Aquinas a power of each soul; moderns divide (Caston divine, Wedin human).
Objection: a deathless part of each person revives dualism; god or one intellect makes the chapter not about the human soul.
Reply (the literature's): thought was flagged in advance as the exception to hylomorphism; each reading still pays a price.

column1: Reconstruct the argument that substance is form (Metaphysics Z.17).
column2:
Premises: substance is a cause, so seek it by a why-question; a real why-question asks why one thing belongs to another, as why these bricks and stones are a house; the syllable BA is more than B and A, and flesh more than fire and earth; the extra something cannot be another element, or a regress follows, nor be made of elements.
Conclusion: form "is the substance of each thing (for this is the primary cause of its being)" (1041b27–28, Ross).
Objections: form may be an empty label; and if no universal is substance (Z.13) while knowledge is of universals, is form universal or particular?
Reply (the literature's): in living things form is the soul, defined by what it does; Frede and Patzig say particular, Woods, Lewis and Code general; treat it as open.

column1: Reconstruct the argument for the unmoved mover (Metaphysics Λ.6–7, 9).
column2:
Premises: if all substances were destructible, everything would be; change and time are eternal, and only circular motion is continuous; a mover that could fail to act guarantees nothing, so there must be a principle whose essence is actuality, without matter; what moves the first heaven must be unmoved; it moves as an object of desire does, "as being loved" (1072b3–4, Ross); its activity is the best, thinking of itself.
Conclusion: a first mover exists of necessity, a living god of self-thinking thought.
Objections: why must the chain stop, and why one mover when Λ.8 counts forty-seven or fifty-five? How can a self-thinking god explain the world?
Reply: the series is ordered per se (a scholastic defence, disputed as Aristotle's); and the world is ordered toward the god, as an army toward its leader.

column1: Reconstruct the function argument (NE I.7).
column2:
Premises: a thing's good lies in performing its function (ergon) well; if carpenter and tanner have functions, presumably a human does too; nutrition and perception are shared with plants and animals; what remains is the active life of the part with reason; a function is performed well in accordance with virtue.
Conclusion: "human good turns out to be activity of soul in accordance with virtue" (1098a16–18, Ross), over a whole life, since "one swallow does not make a summer".
Objection: no maker assigns a whole human life a job, and distinctiveness is not goodness, as elaborate cruelty shows.
Reply (the study guide's): a function is what a thing characteristically does when working well, not a designer's purpose, and the good is rational activity done well. The argument stands or falls with the teleology.

column1: Reconstruct the doctrine of the mean (NE II.6).
column2:
Premises: character virtue concerns feelings and actions, which admit excess, deficiency and the intermediate; the intermediate is relative to us, as six pounds of food is too little for Milo and too much for a beginner; excess and deficiency are failures, the intermediate a success; virtue is the state that chooses the intermediate as the practically wise person would.
Conclusion: virtue is a state concerned with choice, lying in a mean relative to us, each virtue between two vices. Spite, theft and murder have no mean.
Objection: the doctrine is trivial (the right amount) or empty (circular through practical wisdom); Hursthouse adds that many virtues lie on no single scale.
Reply (the study guide's): it is a structural claim, not a decision procedure; the mean is not moderation (Urmson); ethics needs trained judgment.

column1: Reconstruct Aristotle's account of akrasia (NE VII.3).
column2:
Premises: Socrates denied akrasia, but his view contradicts the observed facts; knowing has two senses, having and using; action needs a universal and a particular premise, and one can use the first without the second; passion leaves knowledge had only as by someone asleep, mad or drunk; with two universals present, appetite moves the body.
Conclusion: the akratic person acts against knowledge only in a qualified sense, lacking or merely reciting the particular premise, so Socrates' position seems to result.
Objection: the clear-eyed case Davidson made central seems defined away as a kind of drunkenness.
Reply (the literature's): readings split between qualified ignorance and a real clear-eyed conflict; on both, the akratic person judges the better course and fails to act on it, and their regret is the evidence.

column1: Reconstruct the argument that the contemplative life is happiest (NE X.7–8).
column2:
Premises: happiness is activity of the highest virtue, that of the best thing in us, intellect; contemplation is its activity, directed at the best objects; it is the most continuous, pleasant, self-sufficient and leisured activity, and alone loved for its own sake; the gods' happiness can only be contemplation, so the most godlike human activity is happiest; the life of the other virtues is happy "in a secondary degree".
Conclusion: the contemplative life is happiest, lived in so far as something divine is in us.
Objection: this seems to demote the social, practical life of Books I–IX to second best.
Replies: inclusive reading (Ackrill), dominant reading (Kraut), a real tension (Nagel). Living among others, the contemplative still chooses virtuous acts. The dispute stays open.

column1: Reconstruct the argument for the polis by nature and the argument for natural slavery (Politics I).
column2:
Polis (I.2): household, village and polis grow in stages; the polis is their end, and a thing's nature is its end; so "man is by nature a political animal" (1253a2–3, Jowett), with speech to share the just and the unjust; the polis is prior to the individual, as whole to part.
Objection: a polis is founded, so a product of craft (Keyt). Reply: it is natural as virtue is, completed by habit.
Slavery (I.4–7): ruling and being ruled run through nature; those who differ as body from soul, apprehending reason without having it, are slaves by nature.
Criticism: the factual premise is false, and by Aristotle's own account no one could pick out a natural slave; it contradicts the function argument; and its endoxa were the owners' opinions.

column1: What is substance (ousia) for Aristotle?
column2: Substance is what is most fundamentally real. In the Categories it is the individual, the particular man or horse, neither said of a subject nor present in one (Cat. 5, 2a11–14); species and genera are substances only in a secondary sense. This inverts Plato: the individual is bedrock, and the universal is real as said of individuals. Being is said in many senses, but all point to one central case, substance, as every use of healthy points to a body's health (Met. Γ.2; Owen's focal meaning). So Metaphysics Z opens by asking "what is substance?" and answers form. Not stuff, as in a chemical substance: closer to being-ness.

column1: What are the categories?
column2: The categories (from katēgoria, predication) are the ten highest kinds of thing that can be said: substance, quantity, quality, relation, place, time, position, state, action and affection (Cat. 4, 1b25–27). Examples: man, two cubits long, white, double, in the Lyceum, yesterday, is lying down, has shoes on, cuts, is cut. The other nine depend on substance: a colour is always some substance's colour. Two relations sort things further: some are said of a subject, as the species man of Socrates; others are present in a subject, as a patch of white in a body. Not Kant's categories, which are forms of judgement in the mind.

column1: What is hylomorphism?
column2: Hylomorphism, from hylē (matter) and morphē (form), analyses an ordinary substance as a compound. Matter is what it is made of; form (also eidos) is the organisation that makes that matter a thing of a kind: bronze and the shape of Hermes, bricks and the arrangement that makes a shelter. Matter is relative to a level: bricks are clay given a form, clay is earth and water given a form; whether the ladder ends in a prime matter is disputed. Form does the explaining, since the same bricks could make a wall or a kiln. Against Plato, form is in things, not in a separate realm (Physics; Metaphysics Z).

column1: What are the four causes?
column2: Aitia is often better rendered explanation: an answer to a "why?" question. Physics II.3 sorts the answers into four. Material cause: that out of which a thing comes to be and which persists in it, the bronze. Formal cause: the form or essence, the shape of Hermes. Efficient cause: the primary source of the change, the sculptor's art. Final cause (telos, that for the sake of which): the end, or for a living thing the life it is organised to lead. They are four questions a full explanation answers together, and in natural things three often coincide (Phys. II.7). The final cause is not a wish in anyone's head (Argument 5).

column1: Define potentiality and actuality.
column2: Potentiality (dunamis) is a capacity to be otherwise or to act; actuality (energeia, being at work) is its exercise or realisation. An acorn is actually an acorn and potentially an oak. The pair answers Parmenides: change is not being from nothing but something becoming actually what it already was potentially, and Phys. III.1 defines change on this footing. Two refinements recur: first actuality, an acquired capacity such as a sleeper's Greek, against second actuality, its exercise; and the thesis that "actuality is prior to potency" (Met. Θ.8, 1049b5, Ross), which points toward the unmoved mover. Dunamis names a capacity not being exercised.

column1: What is entelecheia?
column2: Entelecheia is probably Aristotle's own coinage and suggests having one's end within. It is often interchangeable with energeia, but entelecheia leans toward the achieved state and energeia toward the activity. It carries two central definitions: change as the fulfilment of what exists potentially, in so far as it exists potentially (Phys. III.1, 201a10–11; Argument 7), and soul as the first entelecheia of a natural organised body (DA II.1). The distinction between first and second actuality, a capacity possessed and a capacity exercised, is what lets a sleeping animal count as alive.

column1: What is nature (phusis) for Aristotle, and why does it imply teleology?
column2: Nature is "a source or cause of being moved and of being at rest in that to which it belongs primarily" (Phys. II.1, 192b21–23, Hardie and Gaye). A wooden bed has no inner tendency to be a bed; an acorn carries its own principle of growth toward a mature form, so a thing's nature is above all its form. Hence nature acts for the sake of something (Phys. II.8): teeth come out right always or for the most part, not by chance, and purpose needs no deliberation, since "Art does not deliberate" (199b28, Hardie and Gaye). Teleology here is end-directedness built into living things, not an outside designer; how far it reaches is disputed (Sedley).

column1: What is the soul (psychē), and what are its powers?
column2: Soul is what makes a living thing alive, so plants have one: "the first grade of actuality of a natural body having life potentially in it" (DA II.1, 412a27–28, J. A. Smith). Actuality makes it the body's form; first means a capacity possessed, since a sleeping animal lives. Asking whether soul and body are one is like asking about the wax and the stamp's shape. The powers are nested: nutritive (feeding, growth, reproduction) in all living things; perceptive, with desire and movement, in animals, touch being the sense none lacks; rational in humans. Each higher power presupposes the lower, as a square contains a triangle (DA II.3).

column1: What is nous, and what is the active intellect?
column2: Nous is the power by which the soul thinks. Perception receives a form without the matter, as wax takes a seal's shape; thought can receive every form, so it has no bodily nature and is, before it thinks, "not actually any real thing" (DA III.4, 429a23–24, J. A. Smith). DA III.5 distinguishes a mind like matter, which becomes all things, from a mind like a cause, which makes all things, as light makes potential colours actual; this active intellect "is separable, impassible, unmixed" (430a17–18) and alone immortal. Disputed: Alexander made it God, Averroes one intellect shared by all humans, Aquinas a power of each soul (Argument 9).

column1: What is the unmoved mover?
column2: First philosophy studies being as being (Met. Γ) and is also theology, the study of unchangeable substance (E, Λ). Book Λ argues: change and time are eternal; eternal change needs an eternal source; a source with unrealised potential might fail to act; so there is a substance whose being is pure actuality, without matter. It moves the heavens not by pushing, which would change it, but as the loved moves the lover: it "produces motion as being loved" (Λ.7, 1072b3–4, Ross). Its activity is thought of the best object, itself: "its thinking is a thinking on thinking" (Λ.9, 1074b34–35, Ross). It creates nothing, knows no particulars and cares for no one.

column1: What is eudaimonia?
column2: Eudaimonia means flourishing, not a feeling: the final good that human life aims at. The function argument of NE I.7 gives it content: a thing's good lies in doing its characteristic work (ergon) well, and the human work is rational activity, so "human good turns out to be activity of soul in accordance with virtue," judged over a complete life, since "one swallow does not make a summer" (NE I.7, 1098a16–18, Ross). The ladder of soul-powers from the De Anima runs inside the argument. Eudaimonia is an energeia, an activity, not a possession; Book X ranks contemplation, the activity of nous, above the practical life (Arguments 12 and 15).

column1: What is virtue of character, and how is it acquired?
column2: Virtue (aretē) is excellence, what makes a thing do its work well. It comes in two kinds matching two sides of the soul: virtues of intellect, in the part that has reason, come mainly by teaching; virtues of character, in the part of desire and feeling that can listen to reason, come by habit. The theory of nature sets the limit: "Neither by nature, then, nor contrary to nature do the virtues arise in us; rather we are adapted by nature to receive them, and are made perfect by habit" (NE II.1, 1103a23–26, Ross). "We become just by doing just acts" (1103a34–b1), as builders become builders by building.

column1: What is the mean (mesotēs)?
column2: The definition of character virtue: "Virtue, then, is a state of character concerned with choice, lying in a mean, i.e. the mean relative to us, this being determined by a rational principle, and by that principle by which the man of practical wisdom would determine it" (NE II.6, 1106b36–1107a2, Ross). The mean is not a midpoint or moderation. It is the right feeling and action, at the right time, toward the right people, for the right reason, set as the practically wise person would set it. Virtue is a hexis, a settled state built by repeated action. Some acts, such as murder and adultery, have no mean at all (Argument 13).

column1: What is phronēsis?
column2: Practical wisdom (phronēsis) is "a true and reasoned state of capacity to act with regard to the things that are good or bad for man" (NE VI.5, 1140b4–6, Ross). It differs from scientific knowledge (epistēmē), which concerns what cannot be otherwise, and from craft (technē), which aims at a product beyond itself: good action is its own end. Practical wisdom and character virtue need each other. Without virtue, practical wisdom is mere cleverness; without practical wisdom, virtue stays the untutored natural virtue of a bold child. The definition of virtue hands it the last word, and it needs experience. Not prudence in the modern sense of caution.

column1: What is akrasia, and why does it test Aristotle's ethics?
column2: Akrasia is acting against one's better judgement; Ross translates it as "incontinence," meaning lack of self-control. NE VII uses it to test the joint between practical wisdom and character virtue, which the ethics says need each other. Socrates denied it was possible: no one, he said, acts against what he judges best, except through ignorance. Aristotle answers in VII.3 that knowledge can be had without being used, and that passion leaves a person knowing only as someone asleep, mad or drunk knows. The akratic person differs from the self-indulgent one, who endorses his appetites and feels no regret (Argument 14).

column1: Why is the polis natural, for Aristotle?
column2: Households form villages, villages form the polis, the self-sufficient community, "originating in the bare needs of life, and continuing in existence for the sake of a good life" (Pol. I.2, 1252b29–30, Jowett). The argument applies the definition of nature: the city is the end of the earlier associations, and a thing's nature is its end. So "man is by nature a political animal" (1253a2–3, Jowett), more fully than bees, because speech (logos) can show the just and the unjust. A being without a city is either a beast or a god. The city is prior to the individual, as the body is to the hand. The same naturalism yields natural slavery (Argument 16).

column1: What are mimēsis and katharsis in the Poetics?
column2: Imitation (mimēsis) represents human action in words, rhythm and song; humans are the most imitative of animals and learn first by imitating (Poet. 4). Tragedy is its highest form: "an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude" that works "through pity and fear effecting the proper purgation of these emotions" (Poet. 6, 1449b24–28, Butcher). Plot is its soul; the best plots turn on reversal, recognition and an error (hamartia, Poet. 13). Whether katharsis means purgation, purification or clarification is still open. Against Plato's charge of third-remove copying, poetry "tends to express the universal, history the particular" (Poet. 9, 1451b5–7, Butcher).

column1: What are endoxa, and how does Aristotle's method use them?
column2: Aristotle reasons through puzzles. Inquiry starts from the reputable opinions (endoxa) of the many and the wise, sets out the puzzles (aporiai) they produce, and saves as much of the opinion as survives, so a passage that reads like doctrine may be one side of a puzzle. Endoxa are not a majority vote: the wise count more, and every opinion is tested. Beneath the method sits one habit of mind: an important word is said in many senses, so he asks how the senses of being, cause, nature, one, good and prior hang together, his deepest methodological break with Plato. Its risk shows in natural slavery, argued from a slave-holding society's opinions.
